query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a compositionally graded Cu–Ni interlayer between the Cu substrate and the high entropy alloy (HEA) coating will significantly improve metallurgical bonding and overall wear resistance compared to direct HEA deposition on Cu.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) substrate intended for surface protection that requires a wear-resistant coating.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin, compositionally graded Cu–Ni interlayer on the Cu substrate, then apply the high entropy alloy coating followed by an optimized post-deposition annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Wear and friction conditions typical for surface protection applications, including cyclic thermal loads and mechanical stresses at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded Cu–Ni interlayer that gradually transitions the chemical and thermal properties between the Cu substrate and the HEA coating.
generation.mechanism: The Cu–Ni interlayer enhances chemical compatibility and reduces thermal expansion mismatch. It promotes interdiffusion at the interface during annealing, thereby forming a robust metallurgical bond that minimizes defects and residual stresses, ultimately preserving the inherent wear resistance of the HEA.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in adhesion strength and durability of the HEA coating on the Cu substrate, leading to improved wear resistance under applied mechanical and thermal cycling.
generation.baseline: A Cu substrate with a directly deposited HEA coating without any interlayer engineering.
generation.boundary: This approach may be limited by the risk of forming brittle intermetallic compounds if the Cu–Ni gradient is not optimally controlled, and the benefits might be less pronounced if the post-deposition annealing parameters are not appropriately tuned.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition gradient within the Cu–Ni interlayer and the precise annealing conditions needed to maximize interfacial bonding while avoiding deleterious phase formation are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with the graded Cu–Ni interlayer followed by the HEA coating and appropriate annealing, and a control set with direct deposition of the HEA coating on the Cu substrate. Subject both sets to standardized wear tests (e.g., scratch, peel, and cyclic load experiments) under identical thermal and mechanical cycling conditions.
measurements: Quantitative adhesion strength (measured by peel or scratch tests)
Microstructural analysis across the interface using SEM/TEM
Wear rate and surface degradation metrics under cyclic loading
Residual stress measurements at the interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Cu–Ni interlayer do not display a statistically significant improvement in interface adhesion and reduced wear rates compared to the control samples, or if the graded layer leads to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases that compromise performance, the hypothesis should be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. frame.goal: To identify a coating (or interlayer) material that can be metallurgically bonded (i.e. adhered) to the Cu matrix while imparting excellent wear resistance.

decision.trend: Initial efforts in coating development for high wear‐resistance have relied on conventional ceramic or intermetallic layers applied on various substrates. These approaches, however, often suffered from poor adhesion due to chemical incompatibilities and mismatches in thermal expansion. More recent studies using high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have shifted toward advanced deposition techniques such as magnetron sputtering and laser cladding. In these works, post‐deposition annealing has been employed to improve film adhesion on substrates like stainless steel, indicating that the interfacial bonding can be tailored via processing modifications. Even though most studies have focused on substrates other than Cu, the trend shows a move from simply achieving hardness or oxidation resistance toward engineering the interface to obtain a durable metallurgical bond.
decision.unsolved: Despite improved processing methods and adhesion treatments, a key unresolved challenge remains: how to achieve a strong, durable metallurgical bond between a highly wear‐resistant HEA coating and a Cu substrate. The difficulties stemming from differences in crystal structure, thermal expansion, and chemical potential between the Cu matrix and typical HEA coatings have yet to be fully overcome.
decision.lever: Develop and integrate a compositionally graded interlayer—such as a thin Cu-Ni (or similarly compatible) transition layer—between the Cu substrate and the wear‐resistant HEA coating, coupled with an optimized post-deposition annealing treatment.
decision.why: Given that recent work has shown that processing modifications (like post-deposition annealing) can enhance adhesion on other substrates, applying surface/interface engineering to create a graded transition layer directly addresses the unique compatibility issues of the Cu substrate. This lever builds on the trend of designing interfaces to bridge the gap in chemical and thermal properties, thereby achieving a robust metallurgical bond while maintaining the excellent wear resistance expected of HEAs.
